items.title: NFL to Face New Trial Over ‘Sunday Ticket’ $4.7 Billion Verdict
items.summary:
The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals has reinstated a jury's finding that the NFL overcharged subscribers to its out-of-market Sunday Ticket package, reversing the district judge who threw the verdict out. In a ruling issued Friday, a three-judge panel ordered a new trial limited to damages, concluding that the $4.7 billion figure the jury reached cannot stand as calculated.

The case turns on claims that the league and its 32 clubs violated antitrust law by coordinating to grant the NFL exclusive rights to sell out-of-market broadcasts to a single partner. A jury sided with the consumer class at trial in 2024. U.S. District Judge Philip Gutierrez then granted the league's motion to vacate the award, ruling that testimony from the plaintiffs' experts should never have reached the jury.

Much of Gutierrez's reasoning rested on economist Daniel Rascher, who used college football as his model for what the market might look like without the league's restraints, testifying that individual teams and conferences could sell out-of-market rights on their own. The judge called that analysis too speculative. The appeals court disagreed, finding he abused his discretion as gatekeeper. "Opinions are neither unfounded nor unreliable merely because they are impeachable," the panel wrote, adding that such disputes "are for the jury to weigh at trial."

The panel also set a high bar for discarding jury findings, writing that a verdict must stand unless it is clearly unsupported by the evidence, as The Hollywood Reporter noted in its account of the ruling. Still, the court held that the jury's damages number was not grounded in a proper reading of the evidence, which is why the dispute returns to district court rather than simply restoring the award.

The NFL said it is weighing further appellate review. In a statement, the league defended its approach, saying its media strategy "features 100 percent of NFL games broadcast on free over-the-air television in the markets of the participating teams and national distribution of our most popular games, supplemented by many additional choices including RedZone, Sunday Ticket and NFL Plus," and calling it the most fan-friendly model in sports and entertainment. The case now heads back to the lower court for a damages retrial.

items.title: Phoebe Bridgers and Billie Eilish Lend Their Voices to My Chemical Romance’s New Short Film
items.summary:
My Chemical Romance have released an animated short film called "Prelude to the End," made with visual artist Lauren Tsai and built around "The End," the opening track from The Black Parade. The voice cast includes Phoebe Bridgers, Billie Eilish, game designer Hideo Kojima and actor John C. McGinley.

The film follows Astrid, a student at a New England boarding school buried in trash, who tumbles down the school's garbage chute while chasing a lost sketchbook and lands in a strange world where discarded ideas have taken on life. Bridgers voices Astrid's sister and Eilish plays a close friend. Kojima appears as a character identified as the Teacher, with McGinley as the Dean.

Alongside the band's music, the short incorporates a live recording of Pascal Dusapin's Flying River, Violin Concerto, performed by the Utopia Orchestra under conductor Giuseppe Mengoli. Pitchfork reported that the release arrives directly on the heels of the band's 20th anniversary reissue of The Black Parade.

The band plans to screen the film at the Hollywood Bowl on October 30 and 31, the closing pair of a five-night stand at the venue. Those dates belong to a larger tour marking the album's anniversary, a run that began last year and followed a full performance of the record at the When We Were Young festival in 2024.

"Prelude to the End" is out now, with the Hollywood Bowl screenings set for the end of the month.

items.title: Comeback or Farewell? Guns N’ Roses, Black Crowes, and Friends Salute Aerosmith at Hollywood Bowl
items.summary:
Aerosmith returned to a concert stage Friday night at the Hollywood Bowl for "California Dream On: Aerosmith & Friends," the first of two sold-out shows, and left the question of what comes next unanswered. The band had not played a full concert since September 2023, when a larynx injury to Steven Tyler sidelined them. Whether the Bowl run functions as a comeback or a closing statement went unaddressed from the stage.

Rolling Stone, reviewing the show, reported that the night split into two halves: a loose revolving tribute hosted by comedian Bill Burr, followed by full sets from the Black Crowes, Guns N' Roses and Aerosmith. Godsmack's Sully Erna, a fellow Bostonian, opened with early cuts "Make It" and "Lightning Strikes," backed by a house band of drummer Kenny Aronoff, bassist Don Was, Phil X and Nuno Bettencourt.

The guest spots ranged widely. Warren Haynes took on "Lord of the Thighs" and the Rufus Thomas song "Walkin' the Dog" from Aerosmith's 1973 debut. Sammy Hagar's "Helter Skelter," with Chad Smith and Andrew Watt, sat oddly in the program before he recovered with "Draw the Line" and a sign-off of "God Bless Aerosmith." Ann and Nancy Wilson of Heart drew the strongest notices of the opening half with "Janie's Got a Gun."

Billy Idol and Steve Stevens played "Livin' on the Edge," and country singer Eric Church handled "Rag Doll" and "I Don't Want to Miss a Thing." The Black Crowes, who played the Bowl in August, raised the level considerably with "Let the Music Do the Talking," "Nobody's Fault" and "Chip Away the Stone." Guns N' Roses, whom Aerosmith took on the road during the 1988 Permanent Vacation tour, followed.

Aerosmith's own closing set was short. Tyler sounded strong, with Tom Hamilton and Brad Whitford steady behind him and Joe Perry bringing out Hollywood Vampires bandmate Johnny Depp for "Train Kept A-Rollin'." Fireworks ended the night. Fans leaving the Bowl offered their own verdict, one telling the magazine "you take what you can get sometimes," with the band's future "to be continued." The second show follows this weekend.
